title: Engineering Quantum Links: Noise and Quantum-State-Degradation Metrics over Metropolitan Fiber Network
authors: Marcello Caleffi, Laura d'Avossa, Angela Sara Cacciapuoti
abstract: Deploying quantum networks over existing network infrastructures requires the same engineering foundations that underpin classical communications: quantitative models of the channel's noise and of the impairments it imposes on the transmitted information. In this work, we build such a foundation on experimental measurements, grounding the quantum-network counterparts of the two cornerstone metrics of classical link characterization - namely, the SINR and the BER - on a 7.3 km deployed metropolitan-scale fiber-loop interconnecting two campuses of the University of Naples Federico II within the national QuantumInternet.it testbed. On the noise side, we adopt a photon-counting quantum analog of the SINR - in which dark counts constitute the intrinsic noise and the photons generated by classical traffic (through either spontaneous Raman scattering or inter-fiber crosstalk) constitute the interference - and we quantify each contribution directly on the deployed loop. On the bit-error side, we consider the main degrees-of-freedom available to encode a quantum state within an optical photon - namely, polarization, time, and frequency - and we quantify for each degree the channel-induced degradation and its drift over time. These results show that a quantum fiber link, like its classical counterpart, can be captured by a small set of measurable parameters, turning quantum networking over deployed fiber from a physics demonstration into an engineering design problem. Together, they provide the key ingredients of a quantum link budget for the Quantum Internet.
summary: This paper develops an engineering framework for quantum networking by characterizing noise and state degradation over real metropolitan fiber links. The authors adapt classical communication metrics like SINR and BER to the quantum domain, measuring impairments across polarization, time, and frequency. This work transforms quantum networking from a theoretical exercise into a quantifiable engineering design problem for the Quantum Internet.
main_problem: To establish an engineering foundation for deploying quantum networks over existing metropolitan fiber infrastructure by quantitatively characterizing channel noise and quantum state degradation.
main_result: The quantum link can be characterized by a small set of measurable parameters, transforming quantum networking from a pure physics demonstration into a solvable engineering design problem.
method: The authors developed a unified framework by creating quantum analogs of classical metrics (SINR and BER) and applying them to real-world measurements on a deployed fiber loop.
model_or_system: The study uses a 7.3 km metropolitan fiber loop in the QuantumInternet.it testbed, comparing quantum signals (C-band) to classical traffic (O-band). The analysis models noise using a photon-counting SINR analog and state degradation across polarization, time, and frequency using BER analogs.
key_observables: Dark-count rate, interference count from classical traffic, channel-induced degradation, and temporal drift for polarization, time, and frequency.
important_parameters: The link budget is built from measurable parameters, including the ratio of signal to noise/interference counts, and the spectral characteristics of Raman noise.
main_assumptions: The approach assumes the use of a shared physical medium, allocating classical traffic to the O-band and quantum signals to the C-band.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates that quantum state degradation is captured by two complementary descriptions: the SINR analog (noise side) and the BER analog (error side, resolved across polarization, time, and frequency).
paper_structure: The paper builds the foundation by first defining the necessary metrics (SINR/BER analogs), then experimentally measuring noise (dark counts, crosstalk) and state degradation (polarization, time, frequency drift) on a deployed loop, culminating in a comprehensive quantum link budget.
why_interesting: It provides concrete, measurable metrics (like the quantum link budget) that bridge fundamental quantum optics theory with practical, large-scale engineering deployment challenges in quantum communication.

A quantum state propagating through an optical-fiber channel is degraded along a small set of measurable axes, in direct analogy with the impairments characterized in classical links. Two complementary descriptions capture this degradation. On the noise side, the photon-counting quantum-analog of the SINR accounts for the intrinsic noise and the interference introduced by co-propagating classical traffic via spontaneous Raman scattering and inter-fiber crosstalk. FIGURE 2. Experimental framework (not to scale). (Top): the Entangled-Photon Source (EPS) emits polarization-entangled, temporally correlated photon pairs; one member (the so-called idler) is sent to a local reference arm, while the other (the so-called signal) probes the link under test. Their temporal coincidences are recorded by superconducting-nanowire single-photon (SNSPD) detectors read out by a time tagger, and feed the two channel metrics. Using one photon of each pair as a heralding reference enables coincidence-based suppression of background counts, providing the rationale for employing an entangled source rather than a bright classical probe. FIGURE 3. Measured C-band photon count rate generated by spontaneous Raman scattering from a classical signal co-propagating in the O-band at 1310 nm, over the deployed SMF-28 fiber (blue), compared with the Hollenbeck-Cantrell prediction for undoped silica (purple) [7]. The measured spectrum exhibits a characteristic local minimum near 1535 nm that the reference model does not reproduce, with the detected photon count departing from it by up to 19.5%. This minimum identifies the C-band operating point least affected by the co-propagating O-band traffic.
